Transforming Colombo into a Regional Digital Hub via Legal Infrastructure
While Sri Lanka has already established itself as a reputable destination for IT-BPM (Information Technology and Business Process Management) outsourcing, evolving into a true advanced digital and tech hub requires transitioning from cheap labor arbitrage to high-value innovation, fintech, and cross-border digital trade. This leap is fundamentally a legal and institutional challenge.
Here are the five key pillars through which strategic legal development can drive Colombo’s digital transformation:
1. Establishing an Independent Legal Sandbox and Tech SEZ (e.g., Port City Colombo)
The Challenge: Traditional local regulatory frameworks, complex bureaucratic red tape, and foreign exchange restrictions deter major global tech venture capitals and startups.
The Legal Solution:
Operationalize special economic zones (SEZs) governed by an independent legal framework based on English Common Law (widely accepted in international commerce).
Guarantee 100% capital repatriation, complete exemption from exchange controls, and tax holidays for tech startups, venture capitals, and digital service exporters.
Integrate international commercial arbitration centers directly into the zone to ensure fast, predictable dispute resolution without relying on local court delays.
2. Modernizing Digital Economy Laws & Emerging Tech Regulations
The Challenge: Outdated legislative frameworks cannot properly regulate modern digital assets, cross-border cloud computing, or artificial intelligence.
The Legal Solution:
Enact comprehensive, GDPR-aligned data protection laws that allow seamless cross-border data flows with the European Union, UK, and Singapore.
Establish clear legal frameworks for Smart Contracts, Digital Signatures, and Asset Tokenization (enabling real-world asset (RWA) tokenization and blockchain-based infrastructure financing).
Introduce forward-looking AI governance and cybersecurity acts that protect intellectual property while fostering innovation.
3. Standardizing Global Remote Work & Cross-Border Employment Compliance
The Challenge: Hiring international talent or employing local developers for global firms creates complex permanent establishment (PE) risks and tax compliance burdens.
The Legal Solution:
Introduce flexible “Digital Nomad” and specialized tech-talent visa regimes with streamlined tax structures.
Legalize and regulate Employer of Record (EOR) models to make it frictionless for international tech giants to legally employ Sri Lankan engineers without setting up local brick-and-mortar entities.

If you work in cyber security, yesterday's announcement makes for interesting reading.

The government has set out a package of more than £600 million for AI security, cyber defence and domestic AI capability. It includes £60 million for a National Cyber Shield, £120 million for the AI Security Institute and £18 million for a chip design academy. There is also a new AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence in Manchester, run with the NCSC.

The important distinction is that a funding announcement is not the same as a job. Money has been set out, but it takes time to become programmes, contracts and hiring. What it does tell you is where the work is heading over the next few years.

From a defence recruitment perspective, demand is already steady for engineers who understand secure design, product security and cleared environments. A new centre in Manchester adds weight to the North West as a place to build that kind of career.

🚨 Ever joined a Scrum Team and struggled to find the Sprint Goal, Definition of Done, or latest release notes?

The problem might not be your team's communication.

It might be how your team's knowledge is organized. 👇

A well-structured Scrum Team Space in Confluence can help everyone find the right information without searching through endless messages and documents.

Here's a practical structure I'd recommend:
📁 1. Team Charter & Foundations
Team roles, working agreements, DoR, DoD, RACI, and tool access.
📁 2. Product
Product vision, quarterly roadmap, customer journey, epics, and release plan.
📁 3. Requirements Repository
Epic details, user story templates, acceptance criteria, UX designs, API specifications, and data models.
📁 4. Sprint Lifecycle
Sprint Goals, Jira backlog links, demo notes, and retrospective outcomes for each Sprint.
📁 5. Engineering & Delivery
Architecture diagrams, API contracts, coding standards, testing strategy, DevOps pipeline, and release notes.
📁 6. Metrics & Observability
Velocity trends, burndown/burnup charts, cycle time, lead time, defects, and delivery dashboards.
📁 7. Knowledge Base
Onboarding guides, environment setup, troubleshooting, feature walkthroughs, and business FAQs.
📁 8. Stakeholder Zone
Executive summaries, quarterly updates, roadmap views, release notes, and risks with mitigations.
📁 9. Archives
Previous Sprints, deprecated features, and retired diagrams—kept for reference rather than mixed with current work.

💡 The real benefit isn't creating more documentation.

It's making important information easy to find, keeping it current, and helping the team make decisions with the right context.

A useful rule: Jira tracks the work; your team space provides the context and knowledge behind it.

♻️ Save this structure as a reference for your next team workspace setup.

I'm speaking with companies that are using AI for the majority of their new code, taking advantage of today's token prices. If those prices increased dramatically, what's the plan B? 

If the AI bubble bursts, it won't look like 2008. That was a liquidity crisis, and it froze everything. It would look more like 2000, when money went into laying fibre for demand that wasn't there yet.

After the dotcom crash, the companies that laid the fibre went bust, the fibre got sold off cheap, and a few years later bandwidth was cheap enough for things like YouTube to happen. The investors lost and the users won. So what's different now?

The fibre put in the ground was ready before it was needed, but it didn't degrade while demand caught up. Data centres will be fine too: the cabling, power and cooling have a lifecycle of 25 to 30 years. A GPU, however, has maybe three to five years at most, so there's no rebound this time around.  If we hit stormy waters, the chips will be worthless by the time the dust settles.

AI isn't going anywhere. The genie is out of the bottle. But the economics have to change.

Neoclouds could be the first to fall. These are companies borrowing against multi-year contracts and agreeing their costs up front, on GPU hardware that loses value faster than the loan does. There's already talk of some of them being cut off from further funding, as they don't have any real assets other than the GPUs.

The big tech companies can raise money when they need to, and with Anthropic filing to go public yesterday, the biggest labs will soon have the public markets behind them too. In the event of a market correction, they are in the strongest position to consolidate more of the stack, and absorb the smaller players. Apple has long been rumoured to be playing this game: let everyone else take the risk and invest up front, and then swoop in at the last second and grab a bargain.

That's the bit that could hit anyone building with AI. Fewer places to rent compute means fewer people setting the price, and sooner or later that price has to turn a profit. The tokens won't disappear, but once the storm has passed, the cheap ones might.

What's your plan B? As much as I'd love to see it, I'm not sure hiring all the developers back is going to be a smooth ride!

In August, Palantir's CTO told an earnings call: "Remember, only Palantir has FDEs."

He was already wrong when he said it.

Six weeks earlier AWS had committed $1 billion to its own forward deployed engineering team. In May, OpenAI capitalised a standalone consulting company at $4 billion and bought a firm in Edinburgh for its 150 deployment engineers. Anthropic launched one with Blackstone and Goldman Sachs.

The most valuable companies in AI spent 2026 hiring consultants.

That should bother anyone who sells software. The whole model since 2005 was that software scales without people.

Services were what you pushed onto partners.

Here is the number that explains the reversal. Roughly 95% of enterprise AI pilots produce no measurable impact on profit, and the researchers blame integration, not the models. If your customer cannot get a system into production, they do not consume tokens.

So the labs are buying their own demand.

Two things I found digging into what this means closer to home:

1. Infosys grew AI revenue 29% quarter on quarter and cut its full-year guidance to 1-2% in the same breath. The AI work is replacing existing work at a lower price rather than adding to it.

2. Presight in Abu Dhabi has a AED 4.9 billion backlog with 93.5% of revenue on multi-year contracts. Different game entirely, because the anchor customer is the state.

Today's newsletter covers the market size, who the real players are in India and the Gulf, which verticals are actually buying, and six axes on which these firms are trying to differentiate.

In my work, I spend more time understanding how the office handles a task than choosing a tool.

So my suggestion for fresh graduates: pick one small task that repeats in a real office, write down its steps, and make it easier with a simple sheet or tool. Keep that as your example.

If you are a recent graduate, which task would you pick?

An AI model can pass validation and still fail in the business.

A sepsis alert arrives in a workflow nobody has time to monitor. A lending recommendation becomes a decision without meaningful review. A vendor changes a model, and the business misses the consequences.

For the executive team, these are operating-model questions: who decides, what gets checked, and when someone intervenes.
I extend the three-layer sociotechnical model to seven to make those responsibilities visible.

The practical focus is the handoff, where an output becomes someone else’s decision. For each critical handoff, define:
 - One internal accountable owner
 - The evidence required to accept the output
 - The outcome and risk measures to monitor
 -  The triggers for escalation, suspension, and safe fallback

A human reviewer needs the time, information, and authority to challenge the system; without them, accountability exists only on paper.

Buying AI does not transfer these responsibilities. Contracts should specify validation access, change notices, and incident duties, but an internal leader still owns the decision to deploy it.

Strategy sets the value, transformation redesigns the work, and governance keeps both on course.

The carousel applies this to healthcare, lending, wealth management, and hiring. "BEACON: The Definitive Business Guide to AI Strategy and Transformation" covers this in Chapter 15.

A committee can oversee the decision. A named executive must own the outcome.

Honestly, layoffs and workforce reductions are already part of how many IT companies are adjusting—through hiring freezes, smaller teams, attrition, and reorganizations, as well as explicit layoffs. AI gives companies another reason to ask how much labor they need, but it is only one factor alongside slower demand, cost pressure, and past overhiring.

Could some firms eventually wind down their IT businesses and pivot elsewhere? Yes, especially smaller or undifferentiated providers whose revenue depends on selling large volumes of routine labor. 

But a mass exit by major IT companies seems less likely than a change in what they sell: fewer hours of traditional outsourcing, more AI implementation, cloud modernization, cybersecurity, data services, and managed platforms. 

These firms already have customer relationships, contracts, and infrastructure that make reshaping the business more practical than abandoning it.

The harder point is that a company can remain successful while employing far fewer people. Growth in AI-related revenue does not guarantee that displaced workers will be rehired into equivalent roles. 

So even if the industry doesn’t “wrap up,” parts of the traditional IT services model may shrink sharply—and workers may feel that as a real contraction.

I’d put it this way: the day is not far off for some companies to pivot; for the largest firms, the pivot is likely to happen inside the company rather than by leaving IT altogether.

Eight in ten large companies in Europe and the Middle East have already taken an AI incident to the board.

Only four in ten changed their governance policy in response.

That is IBM's data, published last week. It tells you exactly where the next 18 months are heading.

Five governance traps are forming right now. Each one is avoidable. Each one gets more expensive the longer it sits.

	1.	The reprieve trap.
The EU pushed its high-risk AI Act obligations from August 2026 to December 2027. Plenty of boards heard "later". The systems in scope are already making decisions in hiring, credit and education. The general-purpose AI rules never moved. Two new prohibitions land on 2 December this year.
	2.	The sprawl trap.
Large US enterprises now run an average of 183 AI tools. 85% of executives describe them as disconnected. Around a quarter cannot say who coordinates AI across departments. You cannot govern what you have not counted.
	3.	The urgency exception.
47% of senior AI leaders at billion-dollar US companies admit they skipped their own governance process for an urgent deployment. The policy existed. The deadline won.
	4.	The agent gap.
87% of organisations encourage staff to use AI agents. Only 47% have the governance and controls to match. Agents act. They don't just suggest. Liability follows the action.
	5.	The contract shield.
Connecticut's new AI law, live since 1 October, voids contract terms that shield software developers from liability for discriminatory outcomes. "The vendor is responsible" is a weaker defence every month.

Now the uncomfortable part.

These numbers come from companies with compliance departments, risk committees and in-house legal teams. If they are struggling, a healthtech business with 90 engineers and one stretched CTO is not ahead of them.

This is why the 6E Method™ treats governance as architecture, not paperwork.

Evaluate. A full inventory of every AI tool, model and agent in use, sanctioned or not.

Envision. A clear position on risk appetite before a regulator writes one for you.

Empower. One named owner for AI across the business. Not a committee.
Equip. Controls built for agents that take action, not chatbots that answer questions.

Enable. Governance inside the delivery pipeline, so urgency cannot route around it.

Evolve. Every incident changes a policy. Otherwise it was just a bad week.

The companies that come through 2027 cleanly won't have the thickest policy document.

They will have governance that moves at the same speed as deployment.

The UK jobs market is opening up just not in the way many candidates expect.

Vacancies have fallen to 691,000, their lowest level outside the pandemic since 2014, while more people are actively looking for work. At the same time, permanent hiring has shown its first signs of recovery in almost four years.

Translation: there are opportunities but fewer easy ones.

AI has made it simple to apply for 100 roles. It has also made it harder to stand out. UK graduate roles now attract an average of 141 applications, and many candidates are responding by applying even more widely.

The better move? Increase your scope.

•	Look beyond your exact job title. Your skills may transfer into adjacent sectors, functions, or contract work.

•	Target growing pockets, not just familiar ones. IT, engineering, and some permanent private-sector demand are showing more resilience than retail and hospitality.

•	Consider temporary and project roles. Temporary billings are rising, and they can be a faster route into employers that are cautious about permanent hires.

•	Build proof, not just applications. A short portfolio, case study, LinkedIn post, or measurable project outcome beats another AI polished CV.

•	Use AI to think better not to blend in. Let it help you research, tailor, and prepare, but keep your judgement and voice visible.

•	Go where algorithms cannot. Referrals, alumni networks, industry events, and direct conversations remain powerful in a crowded market.

The candidates who succeed will not simply apply more.

They will become more visible, more adaptable, and easier to recommend.
